segments.text: I want to address two ways in which
scrum teams differ from teams on
traditionally managed projects. First,
scrum teams are crossfunctional. Second,
scrum teams are self-organizing. In a
traditionally managed project, each
person has a specific role. The tester
tests, the coder codes, the designer
designs. And if the project needs more
than one person in any of these roles,
the project forms specialized teams. We
might have a test team on the third
floor. Programmers are on the second
floor and the designers, they're not
even in the building. They're from an
outside agency. On a scrum team, we do
it differently. We create what is called
a crossf functional team. A crossf
functional team is made up of
individuals who together have all of the
different skills needed to build
whatever is being developed. So instead
of a test team, a programming team, and
a design team, Scrum will feature a team
that has testers, programmers, and
designers on it. A big advantage to a
crossf functional team is that it is
self-sufficient. It isn't reliant on
another team to do something before it
can begin its work. As an example, think
about the projects I referred to with
designers from an outside agency. The
programmers can't start their work until
the designers finish the designs. And
the testers can't start their work until
the programmers hand over some code.
When teams are structured like this,
there tends to be a lot of waiting time.
Crossf functional teams greatly reduce
waiting time and the effort to manage
dependencies.
A common myth about crossf functional
teams is that each person needs to have
every skill. Not at all. The team as a
whole needs all of the skills to take an
idea from the product backlog and fully
implement it. Sure, it's great to have
team members who could do multiple jobs.
A tester who can do some programming,
for example, but expecting everyone to
have every skill is absolutely not
necessary.
A second way in which scrum teams differ
from traditional teams is that scrum
teams are self-organizing.
A self-organizing team chooses how best
to accomplish its work. Since the team
is closest to the work, we want to give
them the freedom and flexibility to
figure out how to do it. When team
members are empowered to self-organize,
they develop more pride in and ownership
of their work. A common fear around
self-organization is that the team will
just do whatever they want. Management
asks them to build an ecommerce website
and the team decides making a video game
would be more fun.
The first book to mention scrum, wicked
problems, righteous solutions by Peter
Degrace and Leslie Stall addressed this
concern back in 1990. The author said,
"Control is still exercised, but it is
subtle and much of it is indirect.
How a team self-organizes is greatly
influenced by leadership decisions. who
is put on the team, the size and nature
of the challenge given to the team, how
team members are evaluated and rewarded,
how tolerant management is of mistakes
and so on. So self-organizing teams in
scrum are not running a muck working on
whatever team members choose. Rather,
self-organization is about allowing a
team to determine how they will tackle a
problem.
